platforms.title: What Your Urine Smell Is Actually Trying to Tell You
platforms.meta_description: A change in urine smell isn't random — sweet odor, ammonia smell, and cloudy urine each point toward a different cause, from diabetes to infection.
platforms.body_html:
Noticing that urine smells different than usual is easy to brush off, but the specific type of smell is a genuinely useful clue rather than a vague warning. Different odors point toward different underlying causes, and knowing the pattern can help decide how quickly to get it checked.

A Sweet Smell Points Toward Blood Sugar

According to Cleveland Clinic, "pee with a sugary or fruity fragrance can serve as a warning sign of diabetes or high blood sugar." The sweetness comes from the body eliminating excess glucose through urine when blood sugar levels are running high. If this smell shows up alongside increased thirst or more frequent urination, it's worth checking blood sugar rather than assuming it's related to diet alone.

An Ammonia Smell Points Toward the Kidneys, Liver, or Dehydration

Cleveland Clinic notes that "pee with a smell reminiscent of ammonia or bleach can indicate a wide range of health concerns," including kidney disease and liver disease. Simple dehydration is also a common and far less serious cause of a stronger ammonia smell, since concentrated urine naturally smells more pungent than diluted urine — which is why this particular smell is the least specific of the three and benefits most from paying attention to how much water you've actually been drinking before assuming something is wrong.

Cloudy or Foul Urine Points Toward Infection

When an ammonia-like or foul odor comes with visibly cloudy or bloody urine, "the most common [cause] is a urinary tract infection (UTI)," with additional symptoms typically including painful urination and a persistent urge to go. The bacteria responsible for a UTI directly alter both the color and smell of urine, which is why this combination — smell plus cloudiness plus discomfort — is a more specific signal than smell alone. Left untreated, a UTI that has progressed enough to change urine odor can, in some cases, spread toward the kidneys, which is part of why this particular combination of symptoms is treated as more urgent than an odor change by itself.

How to Read Your Own Symptoms

  • Sweet or fruity smell + increased thirst/urination on most days — worth a blood sugar check, especially without a clear dietary explanation. A one-time sweet smell after eating something unusual is less concerning than a pattern that repeats across several days.
  • Ammonia smell alone, otherwise fine — try increasing water intake first and recheck before assuming a kidney or liver issue.
  • Ammonia or foul smell + cloudy/bloody urine + painful urination — this combination points specifically toward a UTI and is worth prompt evaluation.

A smell that persists for more than a couple of days despite adequate hydration, especially with any of the accompanying symptoms above, is a reasonable reason to see a doctor rather than wait it out. Keeping a brief note of when the smell started and what, if anything, changed around the same time — a new medication, a change in diet, or reduced water intake — can make that conversation with a doctor considerably more efficient.

This article is for general health information and is not a substitute for professional medical advice.
